title: Service, training and leadership at Sacred Heart Hospital
author: Dr Peace Ugbodaga, Dr Temitope Joseph and Dr Tolulope Omitade
summary: Selected questions and complete answers from the newsletter’s interview with Sacred Heart Hospital’s Medical Director.

qa.question: Sir, in your few years in oﬃce, you have continued to uphold the remarkable goodwill and legacy of this hospital. Could you kindly share with us the core values that inspired its establishment?
qa.answer: The hospital was formally established in 1895, so it is 131 years old this year. But its story began even earlier. The founding fathers, the SMA Fathers, came to Nigeria around 1880 and started treating patients here. Their colleagues, the OLA Sisters, the Sisters of Our Lady of Apostles—arrived in 1886 and also began caring for patients. Around that time, leprosy was a major concern, so they were given this area for a camp and built a leper colony here. The ﬁrst hospital itself was built close to the palace, where the main hospital was located at the time. That is why, when you drive past the old School of Nursing, you can still recognise what used to be the German Hospital. So, by 1895, the hospital was oﬃcially established there, while the leper colony was here. The two sites operated at the same time. Now, this is a Catholic facility; the hospital belongs to the Catholic Church. Some people visiting for the ﬁrst time assume it is a government hospital because of its size and age, but it is not. Apart from spreading the Gospel of Christ, the Catholic Church also believes strongly in the healing ministry. The hospital was therefore established to contribute to that ministry by treating patients and preventing illness. The founders came as missionaries, and healing was part of their missionary work. That is the foundation on which the hospital has continued to build.

qa.question: What about residency training? Which specialties currently oﬀer residency programmes at Sacred Heart Hospital?
qa.answer: Up to the present, because we have mainly been a secondary-care facility, we have only been doing residency training in Family Medicine. There was a time we tried to introduce residency training in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, but we were not able to meet the requirements. We hope that, as things move forward, we will be able to meet those requirements. For now, we do residency training in Family Medicine. We also provide other forms of training for our healthcare colleagues. We do internship training in nursing, pharmacy and laboratory services, and we have students coming from diﬀerent institutions for training here. We also have a collaboration with Babcock University; their anaesthetic residents come here to increase their exposure. We collaborate with FMC as well, and there was a time some of their Family Medicine residents came here to do their rotations. These are the training programmes we are running for now. But if things move forward, most likely we will be able to introduce residency training in more specialties.

qa.question: How have you sustained professional development through training and retraining, while ensuring that staﬀ have the skills and capacity required to discharge their duties eﬀectively?
qa.answer: With regard to the japa syndrome, it is a major issue, and maintaining clinical standards is also a signiﬁcant challenge. For the doctors, what we have learnt so far is that we must give ourselves a ﬁghting chance. As I mentioned earlier, the salary was poor and it is still not where we want it to be, but we have made some improvements. The diﬀerence between our salaries and those in government hospitals remains quite large, but we have tried to narrow the gap so that we can compete. We may be attracting doctors from other private institutions, but government hospitals are still attracting doctors from us because they pay a little more. We also provide some incentives for our doctors. Unlike many other facilities, we try to oﬀer most of them accommodation within the hospital at little or no cost. Many of us live within the hospital, and that is part of what we have done. They also enjoy some utility beneﬁts. Once you live within the hospital, you do not have to pay for security, electricity or water. So, even if the salary is not as high as what they may earn elsewhere, they can make some savings on those expenses. With regard to training, we learnt over time that one way to retain doctors is to run a residency training programme. That was why the Family Medicine residency programme was started, and we have been trying to keep it going. It helps to keep doctors on the ground because a resident doctor, even if he or she eventually changes location, usually stays longer than a medical oﬃcer. A medical oﬃcer often wants to move elsewhere to begin a residency programme, and that creates instability. So, we try to invest more in residents, even though it is becoming more costly to do so. For the nurses, it has been diﬃcult. As I said, changes in the country's training system have made the traditional School of Nursing route less attractive, as everyone now wants to obtain a BSc to remain relevant. So, even when nurses qualify and we employ them as registered nurses or midwives, many leave within a year. That makes it diﬃcult to build a stable workforce. They may come in today for training, but by tomorrow, they will be gone. It can be discouraging. What we still have are some senior nurses who are willing to remain. For other members of staﬀ, training has not gone as planned, but we hope to improve it. It is one of the areas we want to work on. Even if we cannot send them elsewhere for training, we can arrange in-house training for them. That is the plan and what we hope to do. The only challenge is that it can be painful when you train a group of people and they leave soon afterwards.

qa.question: Thank you for that insightful response, sir. As we bring this conversation to a close, what guiding advice would you oﬀer the younger generation of doctors and other healthcare professionals aspiring to become eﬀective leaders?
qa.answer: Okay, my advice to the younger generation is that people should understand what medicine involves. If you do not have a passion for it, do not bother studying medicine. Some people enter the profession for the wrong reasons or for the money, but medicine is demanding. As I said, if you do not have that passion, do not bother, because along the line, it can become frustrating and diﬃcult. There is money in medicine, but not the kind of money some people expect. As a doctor, you can live comfortably. But if your aim is to make a huge amount of money, you may forget the essence of medicine, which is to care for the sick and the less privileged. That does not mean doctors should not be well cared for, but the goal should not be excessive wealth. Some people want to become millionaires through medicine, but if that is your focus, you may end up compromising on many fronts. Number two, as leaders of the healthcare team, in a family, not all the children will decide to do what their father does. As their father, I will still care for all of them, including the one who chooses farming. So, doctors who are going to become leaders should learn to carry everyone along. Once people see that you have their interests at heart and are concerned about their well-being, they will work with you, and the system will run more smoothly. If you are a doctor who collaborates well with nurses, especially as a medical oﬃcer, your work will be much easier. So, collaborate with them and carry them along. If you do that, people will be less likely to challenge you for the leadership seat. Leadership is diﬃcult, and not everyone truly wants that responsibility.
